subject_line: James and Luke in the autumn of 2002
email_body:
Dear Seán,

Open, Heaven follows a single year that begins when shy sixteen-year-old James meets Luke in the autumn of 2002, and it does so in barely two hundred pages. I was curious how a poet decides what a novel can leave unsaid. Did the compression come from your poetry, or did the story ask for it?

subject_line: The bureau de change on the border in The Bureau
email_body:
Dear Eoin,

The Bureau sets a kidnapping on the Irish borderlands around a bureau de change that is really a laundry for money, with Owen, the owner's son, taken by clients who are owed. I read that the idea started in a conversation with a producer on Vikings: Valhalla. I would love to ask how that chance conversation turned into a book grounded so closely in fact.

subject_line: Ben, rehab and a Balkan property deal in White City
email_body:
Dear Kevin,

White City puts Ben, the son of a disgraced banker, in rehab and then hands him a shady property deal in the Balkans, which feels like a very dark joke about the years after the Celtic Tiger. You've said you were always interested in the private lives of powerful people who fall into disgrace. I'd like to ask how you found the comic register for that material.

subject_line: From an East London staff room in 1996 to Dublin in 2017
email_body:
Dear Hilary,

The Weight of Love opens with Robin and Ruth meeting in the staff room of an East London school in 1996, then jumps to Dublin in 2017, with Joseph's affair with Ruth sitting between those years. Having written plays such as Doldrum Bay and the memoir Hopscotch first, how did you approach the long gap of time that a novel allows and a stage rarely does?

subject_line: Reading your own biomonitoring results as poetry
email_body:
Dear Adam,

Anatomic builds a chemical autobiography out of biomonitoring and microbiome tests of your own body, asking where the inside of a body ends and the outside begins. I'd be curious to hear what it was like to receive those lab results as raw material, and whether any single finding changed the direction of the book.

subject_line: Cold spots as bruises in Letters in a Bruised Cosmos
email_body:
Dear Liz,

You've described how the title Letters in a Bruised Cosmos came from astrophysicists reading cold spots in a heat map of the universe as bruises, other universes pressing against ours. The book sets Anishinaabe sky knowledge beside Western cosmology and neuroscience. I'd like to ask how your early training in science shapes the way a poem of yours begins.

subject_line: Rewriting Cooper's landscapes in Empty Spaces
email_body:
Dear Jordan,

Empty Spaces takes James Fenimore Cooper's landscape descriptions from The Last of the Mohicans and rewrites them on the page, growing out of the visual work in NISHGA. You've recalled watching the 1992 film as a child and feeling you should have seen yourself somewhere in it. I'd like to ask how that early sense of absence turned into a novel built from emptied settler prose.
